title: Torakusu Yamaha's First Organ Looked Right but Was Out of Tune
dek: In 1887 a repairer of medical instruments mended a school's imported organ, built one of his own, and was told in Tokyo it could not be used.

story.event: Repairing a school's reed organ, building his own and going to study tuning after it was rejected
story.summary: In 1887 Torakusu Yamaha, who repaired medical instruments in Hamamatsu, mended an elementary school's imported reed organ and, with the artisan Kisaburo Kawai, built a prototype in about two months. When the Music Investigation Committee in Tokyo judged its tuning too inaccurate to use, he stayed a month to study music theory and tuning, then built a second organ that was accepted. In 1897 he founded Nippon Gakki, renamed Yamaha Corporation in 1987.
paragraphs: In 1887 the reed organ at an elementary school in Hamamatsu, in Shizuoka Prefecture, stopped working. Organs were all imported and hardly any technicians could service one, so the school turned to Torakusu Yamaha, a 36-year-old who repaired medical instruments and watches. Yamaha's American company dates the principal's request to 15 July. Torakusu had trained in watchmaking; by BCN's account, he had never worked on an instrument.

He got the organ working, and as he went he drew its parts. Yamaha's own history describes what he had noticed: alongside reading, writing and the abacus, schools were beginning to teach choral singing to the accompaniment of reed organs, and every one was imported. He judged that many more would be needed and that they could be made in Japan. With Kisaburo Kawai, an ornament artisan, he built a prototype in about two months.

Nobody in Hamamatsu could tell him whether it was any good, so he took it to the Music Investigation Committee in Tokyo, forerunner of the music faculty at Tokyo University of the Arts. There was no railway yet; the company's story, later cast as a bronze relief, has him carrying the organ on a shoulder pole over the Hakone mountains. The verdict was blunt. It had the shape of an organ, he was told, but its tuning was too inaccurate to use.

Realising, as Yamaha puts it, that craftsmanship alone was not enough, he stayed in Tokyo for a month to study music theory and tuning. Back in Hamamatsu he built a second organ and took it to Tokyo. This time he was told it could take the place of imported instruments. Yamaha dates that success to 1887; a 2024 article in Kodansha's Gendai Business puts it in 1888.

His organs gained a reputation. A first company was later wound up, according to the trade news site BCN because a jealous rival forced it, but on 12 October 1897 Torakusu incorporated Nippon Gakki and became its first president. The next year the company adopted a tuning fork as its mark, which Yamaha links to the months he spent learning to tune with one in his hand. In 1987, its centenary year, Nippon Gakki renamed itself Yamaha Corporation.

quote.text: we come into the world with no natural notion of a right-angled triangle, or of a diesis (a quarter tone), or of a half-tone; but we learn each of these things by a certain transmission according to art
quote.locator: Discourses, Book II, Chapter 11, "What the beginning of philosophy is"
quote.source_title: A Selection from the Discourses of Epictetus with the Encheiridion, tr. George Long, Project Gutenberg eBook #10661
quote.connection: Epictetus picks the quarter tone as his example of knowledge nobody is born with: it has to be handed on by people who already have it. Torakusu had skilled hands but had never been taught to tune, and the remedy was not more hours at the bench but a month spent as a student.

reflection: There is a particular sting in being told that your work has the right shape but does not do its job. The natural answer is to work longer at what you already know how to do. Torakusu answered differently: he named the one thing he had never been taught, and went to the people who could teach it.

You will meet verdicts like that, from a customer, a colleague or your own testing. Not all of them will be fair. But some point at a gap that no number of late evenings can close alone, only a conversation with someone who already knows, and asking is not a failure of effort.
invitation: Think of one part of your work where effort is covering for a skill you were never taught. Write down the name of one person who has that skill, and send them a single question today.

sources.title: Origins of the Yamaha Brand
sources.supports: Torakusu's training in watchmaking and work repairing medical equipment for a Hamamatsu hospital; the request from an elementary school in Hamamatsu to repair a reed organ; drawing the inside of the organ while repairing it and building a prototype; the tradition that he carried it over the Hakone mountains on a carrying pole, later made into a bas-relief; harsh criticism of its tuning; studying music theory and tuning; the tuning fork mark inspired by studying tuning with a tuning fork in hand

sources.title: We Begin with a Broken Reed Organ (History of Innovation)

sources.title: Bas-relief: Torakusu Yamaha carrying the organ over Mount Hakone (Innovation Road collection)

research_notes: Most detail comes from Yamaha's own histories, so the story attributes it ('Yamaha's own history', 'as Yamaha puts it') and checks the pivotal points against two independent Japanese outlets (BCN+R, 2017; Kodansha's Gendai Business, 2024). Date of the repair: Yamaha Corporation and both outlets give 1887; Yamaha Corporation of America gives the day as 15 July 1887, attributed in the story. Date of the accepted organ: Yamaha's timeline says he succeeded in the same year, 1887; Gendai says 1888; the story gives both. Company founding: Yamaha Corporation of America's page says he founded Nippon Gakki 'later that same year' (1887) and Wikipedia also says 1887, but Yamaha Corporation's own timeline gives 12 October 1897, matched by Gendai and BCN; the story uses 1897. The first organ company's founding date varies (BCN says 1887; other secondary accounts 1889), so the story gives no date for it, and attributes the reason for its dissolution (a jealous rival) to BCN. The Hakone carry is told by Yamaha as something 'it is said' and by BCN as 'it is also said', so the story presents it as the company's story. The organ is 'imported' in Yamaha's accounts and 'American-made' in Gendai; the story says imported. Kisaburo Kawai, the ornament artisan named by Yamaha's Innovation Road, is not Koichi Kawai, the later founder of Kawai Musical Instruments. Some secondary accounts name Isawa Shuji as the official who judged the organ; no source cited here names him, so the story does not. Yamaha Corporation of America says the company had 100 staff and made 250 instruments a year by 1889; this was not used. Age 36 is BCN's. A Hamamatsu Museum of Musical Instruments newsletter (No. 101, 2015) was reported in search summaries to discuss newer research on the early chronology, but its Japanese text could not be extracted, so it is neither cited nor relied on. The quote comes from Long's selection, which gives chapter titles without numbers; 'What the beginning of philosophy is' is Discourses II.11.
